title: Valuation analysts use AI to gather data and build routine model parts
problem: Routine valuation tasks such as importing annual-report data, adjusting multiples and benchmarking against comparable public companies previously took hours of manual effort.
approach: Big Four valuation leaders told a 2025 conference that AI or robotic automation tools now handle data gathering, formatting and routine modelling.
Analysts focus on interpreting outputs and validating AI-generated results; final valuations stay with people.
No time or cost figures were given (self-reported). Evidence comes from valuation advisory practices, not audit-employed specialists.
who: PwC, Deloitte, KPMG, EY valuation leaders

title: Valuation providers build third-party AI analytics into their methods
problem: Fund managers are asked for faster, more frequent and more traceable valuations under investor and audit scrutiny, often without extra budget or headcount.
approach: CohnReznick announced it is adding 73 Strings valuation analytics to its methods to analyse large data sets (self-reported; no measurements published).
Valutico's April 2026 release adds AI recommendations for peer and transaction selection (vendor-published; no figures published).
Valuation professionals retain judgment on complex inputs and conclusions, and review and select peers and inputs.

title: Valuers use generative AI to draft report sections like market commentary
problem: Valuation reports contain narrative sections such as market commentary, which the valuation standards body counts among the more straightforward tasks AI can automate.
approach: The International Valuation Standards Council says some valuers already frequently use ChatGPT or other public AI to help write report parts.
In other cases, report writing may be a fully automated process within the firm.
The valuer verifies data sources and confirms facts before issuing the report. No outcome figures published (independent).
who: International Valuation Standards Council (no named firm)

title: AI-assisted quality-control review of valuation reports (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: valuation reports must use the correct basis of value, be internally consistent and rest on a complete scope of work.
approach: The International Valuation Standards Council paper suggests AI could review reports for the correct basis of value and for inconsistencies.
It could also check that the scope of work contains all relevant elements.
The valuer or reviewer remains responsible for the report.

title: Agents build complete valuation models; analysts supply and review assumptions (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: the judgment in a valuation model sits in company-specific assumptions, on which professional analysts legitimately disagree.
approach: Researchers report that language-model agents can now construct complete financial models, and built a benchmark from 1,001 professional valuations to grade them.
Agents are far better at building models than at deriving the company-specific assumptions that drive valuation (independent research).
The analyst supplies and challenges the company-specific assumptions.

title: Actuaries use generative AI for analysis and code under model-validation standards (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: actuaries must explain methods and justify assumptions, which opaque 'black-box' language models make difficult.
approach: The American Academy of Actuaries treats generative AI as a model, so the US modeling standard applies and results need validation.
A July 2026 benchmark found frontier models strong on standard actuarial knowledge but much weaker on case reasoning and jurisdiction-sensitive practice (independent).
The actuary vets and validates AI recommendations before applying them.

title: Actuarial audit specialists test a client's AI reserving model (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: black-box reserving models give auditors little visibility, so usual in-model checks of claim development may no longer work.
approach: A Forvis Mazars Ireland actuarial director describes ten steps, including upskilling audit teams in machine learning and benchmarking against traditional reserving methods.
Steps also include testing which inputs drove outputs, assessing model architecture and testing reproducibility (self-reported).
Actuarial audit teams apply expert judgment and professional skepticism on when to use more sophisticated techniques.

title: Actuarial auditors build AI challenger to test a client's reserving model (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: if a client's black-box model claims results traditional methods cannot validate, the auditor has no independent comparison.
approach: The Forvis Mazars author says using one AI model to challenge another could become commonplace in actuarial audit (self-reported opinion).
It could help identify user bias in model selection and design, and requires audit teams to build coding skills.
The specialist judges whether differences between the client's model and the challenger are explained.

title: Auditors obtain AI-use disclosures when management's expert uses AI (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: a specialist's work is technical and often not fully transparent to the auditor, and AI inside an expert's valuation adds opacity.
approach: The valuation standards council says valuers should disclose whether, how and why AI was used; its January 2026 draft would mandate it.
Auditors already evaluate a specialist's data, assumptions and methods, so such disclosures would feed that evaluation.
The engagement partner and team evaluate whether the specialist's work provides sufficient appropriate evidence.

title: Auditors treat a client's significant AI use like complex valuation models (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: clients embed AI in financial reporting while governance is immature, with only 6% of audit partners rating it advanced at their largest client.
approach: The AICPA practice aid says client AI with a significant reporting role may warrant considerations like external specialists and complex valuation models.
The Australian auditing standards board says restricted access to a third-party AI application's logic may be a scope limitation (independent sources).
The auditor remains responsible for the audit and the opinion.

title: AI and data-science experts engaged as auditor's experts (idea) (idea)
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: current specialist guidance gives valuation, actuarial, environmental, legal and tax examples, not AI, yet audit teams need people who can evaluate AI systems.
approach: Nigeria's chartered accountants institute asked the IAASB in July 2025 to add AI and machine-learning experts to its specialist guidance examples.
Big Four job postings requiring AI expertise rose to nearly 7% in 2025 from under 2% in 2022; hiring evidence only (independent).
The auditor evaluates the adequacy of the expert's work for the auditor's purposes.

title: Auditors use a firm-specific language model on a complex inventory valuation task
problem: Complex valuation tasks require auditors to produce correct documentation under time pressure.
approach: A field experiment gave 100 auditors at a global audit firm an inventory valuation task, with or without a firm-specific language model.
Access significantly improved output quality and cut completion time, but not adherence to internal audit guidelines (independent; no figures in abstract).
Gains were largest for active users and did not differ by auditor experience. Human checkpoints are not described.

title: Tax advisers use AI tools: one in use, a generative assistant announced
problem: Tax professionals spend time searching and analysing tax legislation and case law.
approach: KPMG UK already used Blue J's AI to predict tax scenario outcomes for employees to review, in its 3,000-strong tax team.
KPMG says the predictive tool forecasts outcomes with 90%+ accuracy (self-reported); this is not the generative product.
In February 2024 KPMG UK and Blue J announced they will launch Ask Blue J, a generative AI tax assistant.
Tax professionals review outputs and advise clients. This is tax advisory, not audit tax specialists.

title: Automated recalculation and sensitivity testing of management's impairment models (Deloitte UK)
problem: Impairment is a judgemental, higher-risk area, and recalculating management's cash-flow models and running sensitivities by hand takes time away from the assumptions that matter.
approach: Deloitte UK says it deployed automated impairment modelling across its largest audits, recalculating models and running sensitivities.
In consumer-business audits it ran the modelling across ten entities and identified several calculation inaccuracies (self-reported; error count not given).
Practitioners apply professional judgement to flagged patterns; impairment specialists provide independent challenge. Deloitte plans to extend it to going concern.
